glance: 200 km to Pirojpur by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
atghar-kuriana-floating-market.desc: In the guava season, farmers paddle their canoes loaded with fruit from the orchards along Swarupkathi's canals to the markets at Atghar and Kuriana. Wholesalers buy directly on the water, and the fruit goes onto bigger boats and trucks to cities. Canals lined with guava orchards make a lovely boat ride. It is one of the most photogenic river markets in Bangladesh.
blocks: How to get there
From Barishal or Pirojpur, travel by road to Swarupkathi, then a local boat or auto to Atghar-Kuriana.
Good to know
Arrive early morning, roughly July to August, for the busiest trade; carry a dry bag for your phone.

atghar-boat-market.desc: In this region of canals, a small boat is as essential as a bicycle elsewhere. Before and during the monsoon, Atghar hosts boat markets where carpenters sell newly built wooden canoes. Buyers inspect the planks, bargain and paddle their new boats home. It is a living example of the area's water-based life.
blocks: Good to know
Ask locally for market days, which are fixed by the week.

glance: Approx. 30–60 BDT per kg in season
Local markets around Swarupkathi and Pirojpur
pirojpur-amra.desc: Pirojpur and neighbouring Jhalokathi are the main amra-growing area of Bangladesh. The crisp, sour fruit is eaten raw with salt and chilli, turned into pickles or cooked into chutney. In season, boats and trucks carry amra from orchards to markets nationwide. Try it fresh from local markets.

glance: 200 km to Pirojpur by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
nazirpur-floating-gardens.desc: When the low beels of Nazirpur stay under water for months, farmers build long floating beds, called dhap or baira, from water hyacinth bound with bamboo and banana stems and topped with soil. On them they raise seedlings of gourd, aubergine, papaya, chilli, cauliflower and more, then sell them at markets such as Baithakata, where a floating vegetable market has run on the Beluya river for decades. Hundreds of families here still work this way, and the system is recognised by the FAO as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System. In season the green rafts stretch across the water, with women tying seedlings into small root balls on the verandas. Few outsiders come to see it.
blocks: How to get there
From Pirojpur go by road to Nazirpur and on to Baithakata (Mugarjhor) in Malikhali union, then hire a small boat to move among the beds.
Good to know

Bed building starts around mid-May and runs through the monsoon. Time your visit for Baithakata's floating market days (Saturday and Tuesday). Ask farmers before going near the beds, and buy a few seedlings or vegetables if you can.

glance: 200 km to Pirojpur by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
baleshwar-riverfront.desc: The Baleshwar is one of the great rivers of the south-west, flowing past Pirojpur towards the sea. Its banks see ferries, cargo boats and fishermen at work. The wide water and big skies are best appreciated at sunset from the river ghats. Hilsa and other fish are landed along its course.
blocks: How to get there
Reach the river ghats near Pirojpur town by auto.
Good to know
River conditions change with tide and weather; use only licensed ferries.

glance: Baithakata floating market on the Beluya river, Nazirpur (Saturdays and Tuesdays)
nazirpur-floating-garden-vegetables.desc: In Nazirpur's low beels, which stay flooded for months, farmers pile water hyacinth and weeds into floating beds and grow vegetables and seedlings on them without chemical fertiliser. The practice is said to be about two centuries old and has been recognised by the UN's FAO. Twice a week farmers bring the produce by boat to the floating market on the Beluya river beside Baithakata bazar.

glance: 200 km to Pirojpur by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
momin-mosque.desc: In 1913 Momin Uddin Akon, a villager of Burirchar in Mathbaria, set out to build a mosque close to home. He first made bricks, then switched to timber so it would match the wooden houses around it. About two dozen craftsmen, many from the Swarupkathi area, spent some seven years fitting the panels together without nails, carving and painting leaves, flowers, pineapples and Arabic calligraphy in natural colours. The prayer hall is small, room for only about thirty people. The Department of Archaeology listed it as a protected monument in 2003, and it remains one of the finest pieces of wooden religious architecture in the country.
blocks: How to get there
From Pirojpur take a bus to Mathbaria, then an auto or motorbike to Burirchar village.
Good to know
It is a working mosque and fragile: dress modestly, take off shoes, avoid prayer times and don't touch the painted panels.

glance: 200 km to Pirojpur by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
rayerkathi-zamindar-bari.desc: Rayerkathi, just north of Pirojpur town, was the seat of a local zamindar family. The estate holds mansions, temples and ponds in various states of decay, with trees growing from the brickwork. Some temples are still in use by local worshippers. It is an atmospheric place for a short heritage walk.
blocks: How to get there
A short auto or rickshaw ride from Pirojpur town.
Good to know
Avoid entering unsafe buildings; ask permission before entering active temples.

glance: 200 km to Pirojpur by road, 5–7 hours by bus or car
swarupkathi-nurseries.desc: Swarupkathi, also called Nesarabad, is known for its plant nurseries, which supply saplings across the country. Rows of seedlings grow on raised beds between canals, and boats loaded with plants move along the waterways. The town is also a timber trading centre. A slow boat ride shows a side of rural trade few visitors see.
blocks: How to get there
By road from Pirojpur or Barishal to Swarupkathi town, then a hired boat.
Good to know
Combine with the floating guava market on the same day.

glance: Approx. 20–50 BDT per kg in season
swarupkathi-guava.desc: The guava orchards of Swarupkathi are among the oldest and largest in Bangladesh. The fruit is crunchy and sweet, eaten fresh or with salt and chilli. In season, guavas are so plentiful that prices drop sharply at the floating markets. Buying straight from a farmer's boat is part of the fun.
